\begin{abstract}

in place of XGBoost (Table~\ref{tab:alt-classifier}).
All other settings (the same 7 features, 3-class labels, and class-balanced downsampling) are

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 across three classifiers. Each column shows the held-out generator F1. (6-generator LOGO; 3-class.)}
\label{tab:alt-classifier}

\toprule
Classifier & Avg F1 & OLMo-2 & Py-1B & Py-2.8B & Qw-0.6B & Qw-1.7B & Qw-8B \\
\midrule
XGBoost          & 0.789 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.824 & 0.806 & 0.683 \\

Both tree-based classifiers achieve LOGO F1 $\approx 0.79$,
and even a linear model reaches $0.725$, well above the $0.33$ chance baseline for
three classes.
The per-generator ranking is also consistent across classifiers
(Pythia-1B easiest, Qwen3-8B hardest),
confirming that discriminative power originates in the entropy and lexical features,
not in classifier capacity.

\subsection*{Sampling Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{app:sampling-sensitivity}

To assess robustness to decoding hyperparameters, we regenerate Qwen3-1.7B continuation chains under three sampling configurations (the remaining five generators retain their default-configuration data) and re-evaluate the 6-generator LOGO pipeline (Table~\ref{tab:sampling-ablation}).

Default    & 0.7 & 0.90 & 0.788 & 0.799 & $-0.602$ \\
High       & 1.0 & 0.95 & 0.726 & 0.733 & $-0.002$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Both tree-based classifiers achieve LOGO F1 $\approx 0.79$,
and even a linear model reaches $0.725$, well above the $0.33$ chance baseline for
three classes.
The per-generator ranking is also consistent across classifiers
(Pythia-1B easiest, Qwen3-8B hardest),
confirming that discriminative power originates in the entropy and lexical features,
not in classifier capacity.

\subsection*{Sampling Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{app:sampling-sensitivity}

To assess robustness to decoding hyperparameters, we regenerate Qwen3-1.7B continuation chains under three sampling configurations (the remaining five generators retain their default-configuration data) and re-evaluate the 6-generator LOGO pipeline (Table~\ref{tab:sampling-ablation}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Depth classification under varying sampling parameters. All other settings match the default pipeline. (6-generator LOGO; 3-class and binary.)}
\label{tab:sampling-ablation}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc ccc}
\toprule
Config & Temp.\ & Top-$p$ & 3-class F1 & Binary F1 & $\rho$(entropy\_mean) \\
\midrule
Low        & 0.5 & 0.80 & 0.785 & 0.797 & $-0.694$ \\
Default    & 0.7 & 0.90 & 0.788 & 0.799 & $-0.602$ \\
High       & 1.0 & 0.95 & 0.726 & 0.733 & $-0.002$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The depth signal is robust to moderate sampling variation: low and default configurations differ by at most 0.3\,pp in both 3-class and binary F1, and entropy--depth Spearman correlations remain strongly negative ($\rho \leq -0.60$).
At high temperature ($t{=}1.0$, top-$p{=}0.95$), classification degrades by approximately 6\,pp and the entropy--depth correlation collapses to near zero ($\rho = -0.002$).
This is consistent with the hypothesis that depth features are shaped by the sampling mechanism (\S\ref{sec:discussion}): elevated temperature injects sufficient randomness to flatten the distributional drift that accumulates across generation steps, effectively masking the depth signal.
The practical implication is that depth fingerprinting applies reliably under standard decoding regimes but should not be expected to generalize to high-entropy sampling settings.

The 7-feature ensemble achieves the highest unperturbed binary F1 (0.695), but LD-Score surpasses it under perturbation due to near-zero degradation ($-$0.6\,pp across the full 0\%$\to$20\% range).
FastDetectGPT and Avg-LogProb exhibit non-monotonic degradation at higher perturbation rates, likely because severe perturbation introduces distributional artifacts that these token-level methods detect as anomalous.
Avg-LogProb is the most fragile overall ($-$34.7\,pp at 10\%), while FastDetectGPT drops sharply at 5\% ($-$13.4\,pp) before partially recovering.
LD-Score is nearly invariant to perturbation, consistent with its reliance on corpus-level distributional divergence rather than per-token likelihoods.
The 7-feature ensemble offers the highest starting performance among single-reference methods, with sublinear degradation ($-$10.4\,pp at 20\%).

\paragraph{LLM-simulated sentence regeneration.}
To test robustness under semantically coherent editing, we use Qwen3-0.6B-Base to randomly regenerate 1--3 sentences per passage (avg 1.69 sentences, ${\sim}$50\% edit distance) and re-evaluate the 8-gen LOGO pipeline.
Binary F1 drops from 0.692 to 0.647 ($-$4.5\,pp, 6.5\% relative); 3-class F1 drops from 0.739 to 0.667 ($-$7.1\,pp, 9.7\% relative).
The binary degradation ($-$4.5\,pp) is nearly identical to that caused by 5\% random word replacement ($-$4.6\,pp), despite the LLM rephrase altering ${\sim}$50\% of characters.
This asymmetry arises because LLM-generated replacements preserve the underlying statistical fingerprint of the generation process (entropy dynamics, depth-accumulated distributional drift), whereas random word substitution directly destroys local statistical signals.
Depth fingerprinting thus captures deep generative structure that survives semantic-preserving edits.

\paragraph{Seed complexity.}
Performance is stable across seed text complexity: stratifying seeds by vocabulary richness (TTR terciles) yields maximum F1 variation of 1.1\,pp across groups.

We analyze the distribution and characteristics of binary classification errors (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) across the 8-generator LOGO evaluation ($N$\,=\,29{,}095 samples, overall error rate 28.08\%).

\paragraph{Error asymmetry.}
Errors are heavily asymmetric: 86.2\% are false negatives (gen-2+ predicted as gen-1) and only 13.8\% are false positives (gen-1 predicted as gen-2+).
The classifier systematically under-predicts depth, consistent with the DDR framework: shallow gen-2+ samples that have not yet accumulated sufficient distributional drift are indistinguishable from gen-1.

\paragraph{Per-depth error rates.}
Error rates decrease monotonically with depth: depth-2 samples are the primary failure point (48.42\% error rate), followed by depth-3 (29.17\%) and depth-4 (20.32\%).
Depth-1 false positive rate is 7.11\%.
The monotonic decrease confirms that deeper generations accumulate progressively stronger fingerprints, making the gen-1$\to$gen-2 transition the hardest to detect.

\paragraph{Per-generator variation.}
Table~\ref{tab:error-by-gen} shows error rates vary substantially across generators, correlating with model scale: larger models (Mistral-7B, Qwen3-8B) produce text closer to gen-1 characteristics, making depth discrimination harder.

\paragraph{Feature-level explanation.}
Mann-Whitney U tests comparing correctly vs.\ incorrectly classified samples reveal that drifting features show significant distributional differences between correct and incorrect predictions: entropy\_mean ($p < 10^{-300}$), TTR ($p < 10^{-300}$), and hapax\_ratio ($p < 10^{-300}$).
In contrast, shape features show no discriminating power: entropy\_max ($p = 0.584$) and tail\_decay ($p = 0.653$).
